follow_up.question: What happens as the stake approaches the whole bankroll with positive loss probability?
follow_up.reference: A loss leaves wealth near zero. Its log contribution tends downward without bound.

instances.text: Stake 50 percent of current bankroll. Win probability is 70 percent; a win adds 4 times the stake, a loss removes the stake. A calculator is allowed. What is expected natural-log bankroll growth per play, rounded to six decimal places?
instances.spoken_text: Stake fifty percent of current bankroll. Win probability is seventy percent; a win adds four times the stake, a loss removes the stake. A calculator is allowed. What is expected natural-log bankroll growth per play, rounded to six decimal places?

follow_up.question: Why is the log of expected wealth not expected log growth?
follow_up.reference: The logarithm is nonlinear and concave. Averaging after taking logs gives a different and generally smaller value.

instances.text: Stake 40 percent of current bankroll. Win probability is 50 percent; a win adds 2 times the stake, a loss removes the stake. A calculator is allowed. What is expected natural-log bankroll growth per play, rounded to six decimal places?
instances.spoken_text: Stake forty percent of current bankroll. Win probability is fifty percent; a win adds two times the stake, a loss removes the stake. A calculator is allowed. What is expected natural-log bankroll growth per play, rounded to six decimal places?

follow_up.question: Why does a losing round contribute a negative log term?
follow_up.reference: It leaves a bankroll multiplier below one. Ignoring that term would treat losses as if the bankroll were unchanged.
